key_points.point: The document argues for leveraging state-of-the-art privacy-preserving technologies and decentralized machine learning to empower workers. By embedding these technological capabilities into institutional frameworks, it seeks to transform collective labor rights into active, data-driven capabilities. This approach views AI innovation as a tool that, if properly directed, can provide workers with a necessary counter-voice and epistemic agency in the workplace.
key_points.verbatim: This article demonstrates how leveraging state-of-the-art innovations in the technical field of privacy-preserving technologies and decentralising machine learning can provide workers with collective epistemic abilities, which could mitigate violations of their rights in the workplace and enable them to have agency in the workplace.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve worker agency by embedding privacy-preserving technologies and decentralized machine learning into institutional labor frameworks.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for the integration of advanced privacy-preserving and decentralized machine learning technologies into labor institutions to empower workers with collective epistemic capabilities. Encompasses: privacy-preserving technologies, decentralized machine learning, and collective epistemic agency.

key_points.point: The document proposes leveraging decentralised machine learning architectures and privacy-preserving data queries to enable workers to extract value from shared data. This approach views technological innovation as a tool for empowering collective agency rather than merely a source of risk. By integrating these technical affordances into labor law, the author seeks to transform data from a tool of employer control into a resource for worker-led insight. This aligns with accelerationist interests in utilizing advanced computing to solve social coordination problems, though it focuses on labor empowerment rather than pure abundance.
key_points.verbatim: From a technological point of view, while contemporary centralised data architecture tends to suck data from individuals and transfer them to central servers, new and evolving decentralised machine learning architectures and privacy-preserving data queries can facilitate affordances for individuals to collaborate and extract insights from their shared data.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve worker empowerment by deploying decentralised machine learning architectures and privacy-preserving data queries to facilitate collective data analysis.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for the deployment of decentralised machine learning and privacy-preserving technologies to enable collective data-driven value extraction. Encompasses: Decentralised machine learning architectures, privacy-preserving data queries, and collective data-driven affordances.

key_points.point: The document argues that decentralised machine learning architectures, such as federated learning, can enable parallel data processing by both employers and workers. This approach allows for the extraction of value from data by multiple parties simultaneously while maintaining privacy. By democratizing access to data-driven insights, this model promotes a more competitive and diverse data processing landscape. This aligns with accelerationist goals of increasing the utility and accessibility of AI systems.
key_points.verbatim: In this space, decentralised machine learning architectures can open new options to help break down the exclusion of workers from their collective personal data by enabling both workers and employers to utilise the same dataset in parallel (Shadmy & Ligett, 2024).
key_points.canonical_proposition: Implement decentralised machine learning architectures to enable parallel data processing and value extraction by both workers and employers.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for the deployment of decentralised machine learning architectures to facilitate simultaneous, multi-party data utilization. Encompasses: Federated learning, parallel data processing, and competitive data value extraction.

key_points.point: The document argues that workplace data management can serve as a catalyst for the development of privacy-preserving and decentralized AI technologies. By creating legal incentives for collective data access, the author suggests that developers will be motivated to produce more democratic and balanced data management systems. This approach views the workplace as a specific use case that can drive technological innovation, which can then be applied to other domains. The author acknowledges that these technologies are not yet mature but emphasizes their potential to solve power imbalances.
key_points.verbatim: While these barriers should not be ignored, the workplace use case can serve as a significant catalyst for the development of such technologies. Herein lies the great potential of law and technology interoperability. If the law adopts and incentivises — in legislation, regulation, and court rulings — the right of workers to receive a collective epistemological view of the processing of private data in the workplace, then developers will have new incentives and a use case to develop such technologies.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve the development of democratic data management systems by incentivizing the creation of privacy-preserving technologies through workplace-specific legal mandates.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that leverages workplace data governance as a strategic use case to accelerate the development and adoption of privacy-preserving and decentralized AI architectures. Encompasses: law-technology interoperability, incentivizing technological innovation, and scaling democratic data management models.

key_points.point: The document cites research by Villalobos et al. (2022) regarding the potential exhaustion of high-quality human-generated training data. This reflects an empirical concern within the AI development community about the physical and informational limits of scaling machine learning datasets. The inclusion of this reference acknowledges the technical constraints that accelerationists must address to maintain progress.
key_points.verbatim: Villalobos, P., Sevilla, J., Heim, L., Besiroglu, T., Hobbhahn, M., & Ho, A. (2022). Will we run out of data? An analysis of the limits of scaling datasets in machine learning. ArXiv.
key_points.canonical_proposition: The scaling of machine learning datasets faces empirical limits due to the potential exhaustion of high-quality human-generated training data.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that identifies the finite nature of high-quality human-generated data as a potential bottleneck for future model scaling. Encompasses: Data scarcity, scaling laws, and training data quality.

key_points.point: The document asserts that the rapid adoption of data-driven management systems creates a systemic loss of visibility and control for workers. It notes that information is captured from devices and transferred to inaccessible remote servers, leading to opaque, data-driven systems that monitor and regulate workers without their knowledge or control.
key_points.verbatim: Information is automatically captured from workersÆ devices and detectors in the workplace, transferred to inaccessible remote servers, and subjected to secondary uses and processing beyond workersÆ knowledge or control. As a result, labour relations are increasingly mediated by opaque, data-driven systems, which monitor and regulate workers.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Data-driven workplace management systems create systemic opacity and loss of control over worker data.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within safetyist discourse that the rapid deployment of data-driven management systems undermines organizational visibility and control by centralizing worker data in inaccessible, opaque systems. Encompasses: opaque management systems, data centralization, and loss of worker control.

key_points.point: The document asserts that current data-driven management treats employees as objects to be optimized, which degrades their dignity and autonomy. By constantly extracting data to fine-tune models for worker replacement, employers reduce human workers to mere inputs for algorithmic efficiency. This creates a cycle of chronic helplessness and insecurity, as workers cannot anticipate how they will be understood or evaluated by opaque systems.
key_points.verbatim: In such data-driven environments, where individualsÆ automatic profiles determine their benefits and constraints, workers become unable to anticipate the ways in which they will be understood, which means that their agency and autonomy are endangered.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Data-driven management systems treat workers as objects to be optimized, thereby degrading human dignity and autonomy.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within safetyist discourse that algorithmic management frameworks reduce human workers to objects for optimization, undermining individual agency and dignity. Encompasses: Algorithmic profiling, chronic helplessness, and the erosion of worker autonomy.

key_points.point: The document suggests that workers should conduct continuous, independent risk assessments of AI systems in the workplace. By combining collective data with qualitative information on worker well-being, labor organizations can identify harms that are difficult to predict, such as psychological or emotional impacts. This strategy serves as a necessary check on the self-assessments currently provided by software vendors.
key_points.verbatim: Labour organisations could be better positioned to examine the ongoing impact of such systems. Through access to the collective data of workers, combined with qualitative data on the mental and physical state of workers, workers can conduct continuous assessments of the risks related to these systems.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Mandate worker-led, continuous risk assessments of AI systems to supplement or replace provider self-assessments.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that advocates for independent, worker-led monitoring of AI impacts to ensure safety and accountability. Encompasses: Continuous risk assessment, qualitative worker data, and oversight of vendor self-assessments.

key_points.point: The author advocates for integrating labor law with AI governance to address the systemic lack of transparency in high-risk workplace systems. By requiring employers to provide workers with collective access to data flows and model logic, the author proposes a regulatory framework that ensures accountability. This approach seeks to move beyond current 'self-assessment' models of risk, which the author argues are insufficient for protecting employees from algorithmic harm.
key_points.verbatim: The EU AI Act defines workplace systems as 'high-risk systems'; as such, it imposes transparency requirements that oblige the saving of system logs and the performance of risk assessments. However, these obligations are directed mainly to software providers and not to employers; thus, they do little to provide workers with any rights to process the data or even access to it.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Establish legal frameworks that mandate collective worker access to workplace AI system logs and risk assessments to ensure accountability.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that advocates for the expansion of regulatory accountability frameworks to include mandatory collective worker access to AI system logs and risk assessments. Encompasses: high-risk system governance, transparency mandates, and stakeholder participation in algorithmic auditing.

key_points.point: The document references research on 'predictive privacy' and 'collective data protection' by Muehlhoff (2023), supporting the safetyist desire to treat digital space as a public trust. This perspective emphasizes that data protection must move beyond individual control to address the systemic risks posed by AI and big data. It advocates for frameworks that protect collective interests against the invasive nature of predictive analytics.
key_points.verbatim: Mⁿhlhoff, R. (2023). Predictive privacy: Collective data protection in the context of artificial intelligence and big data. Big Data & Society, 10(1).
key_points.canonical_proposition: Digital infrastructure and data protection ought to be managed as a collective public trust to mitigate the risks of predictive AI.
key_points.attribution_text: A Desire within safetyist discourse that advocates for collective data protection frameworks to counter the risks of predictive analytics. Encompasses: Predictive privacy, collective data rights, and systemic data protection.

key_points.point: The document posits that technological asymmetries in the workplace exacerbate power imbalances between employers and employees. It argues that employers use aggregated personal data to position workers as unwitting data providers, thereby limiting worker agency and reinforcing structural power disparities.
key_points.verbatim: Technological asymmetries in data-driven workplaces increasingly shape power dynamics between employers and employees. Employers now extract significant value from aggregated personal data, positioning workers as unwitting data providers and limiting workersÆ agency.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Technological asymmetries in data-driven workplaces systematically shift power from workers to employers.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that algorithmic management systems function as tools of control that exacerbate power imbalances between employers and workers. Encompasses: technological asymmetries, value extraction, and worker agency.

key_points.point: The author proposes 'Data-Driven Collective Affordances' as a mechanism to enable workers to process and interpret their aggregated data collectively. This strategy aims to allow workers to co-determine data use, challenge exploitative practices, and restore balance in data-centric workplaces.
key_points.verbatim: This article introduces the concept of ôData-Driven Collective Affordancesö ù technological mechanisms enabling workers to process and interpret their aggregated data collectively. By embedding these capabilities into legal and institutional frameworks, workers can co-determine data use, challenge exploitative practices, and more effectively exercise their rights.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Establish Data-Driven Collective Affordances to enable workers to collectively process data and challenge exploitative practices.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within skeptic discourse that seeks to redistribute the infrastructural control and financial benefits of AI systems to workers through collective data processing mechanisms. Encompasses: Data-Driven Collective Affordances, collective data processing, and co-determination of data use.

key_points.point: The document observes that AI integration is not merely about job displacement but involves a multifaceted transformation of labor relations. It highlights how employers use personal data to monitor, evaluate, and track employees, and to develop automation that threatens to replace workers.
key_points.verbatim: The increasing collection of personal data is accompanied by an increasing processing of the data to manage, evaluate, and track employees. Employers can also use workersÆ personal data to fine-tune general models and adapt them to the particular enterprise while threatening to replace workers with automated bots.
key_points.canonical_proposition: AI integration reshapes labor by enabling pervasive monitoring, evaluation, and the threat of worker replacement.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that AI integration systematically reshapes work through pervasive monitoring, performance evaluation, and the threat of automation-driven displacement. Encompasses: workplace surveillance, automated evaluation, and labor displacement.

key_points.point: The document argues that algorithmic management systems systematically shift power from workers to employers by creating information asymmetries. Because these systems are opaque and lack concrete explanations for their decisions, employees are unable to understand the logic governing their employment conditions or consent to them. This effectively strips workers of the ability to challenge discriminatory outcomes or anticipate management actions.
key_points.verbatim: Therefore, when employers decide to activate complex machine learning systems for employee management, they actually decide that workers do not fully understand management methods or relational contract conditions and do not consciously have the ability to consent to their employment contracts.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Algorithmic management systems create information asymmetries that shift power to employers and prevent meaningful worker consent.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that algorithmic management functions as a mechanism of control that exacerbates power imbalances through information asymmetry. Encompasses: Opaque management logic, lack of informed consent, and the erosion of relational contract conditions.

key_points.point: The document highlights that machine learning models in the workplace reproduce and amplify discrimination. Because these systems cannot provide concrete explanations for their rankings or limitations, employees are left without the tools to identify or contest discriminatory treatment. This creates a systemic barrier where bias is embedded in the infrastructure of work without being visible to those it affects.
key_points.verbatim: Therefore, making workplace decisions on the basis of machine learning models, which cannot provide concrete explanations for concrete decisions, may produce discrimination without employees having the tools to locate and be aware of such discrimination.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Algorithmic workplace decisions produce and reproduce discrimination that is opaque and difficult for employees to identify.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that algorithmic systems systematically reproduce discrimination while obscuring the causal mechanisms from affected employees. Encompasses: Algorithmic bias, lack of explainability, and structural discrimination in workplace decision-making.

key_points.point: The author proposes 'Data-Driven Collective Affordances' as a policy framework to redistribute power in the workplace. By institutionalizing collective rights through labor organizations, workers can gain the epistemic and productive capacity to audit employer data usage and derive value from their own data. This shifts the control of aggregated datasets from powerful entities to the workers themselves, using labor law as the institutional foundation for data governance.
key_points.verbatim: This article suggests adding another layer to worker collective powers, by translating employeesÆ collective rights into Data-Driven Collective Affordances.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Establish Data-Driven Collective Affordances to redistribute control over workplace data and empower workers through collective epistemic rights.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within skeptic discourse that advocates for the creation of collective data-governance mechanisms to redistribute power and value from employers to workers. Encompasses: Data-driven collective affordances, collective epistemic rights, and the institutionalization of worker-led data auditing.

key_points.point: The document asserts that current power relations in the workplace allow employers to treat employee data as an economic asset while excluding workers from the benefits of that data. This creates a significant power imbalance, as employers use this data to train systems that may eventually replace the workers themselves. The author argues that this exploitation is a structural issue inherent in current data-driven management.
key_points.verbatim: Contemporary power relations shape the allocation of surplus value from workersÆ personal data utilisation (Aloisi, 2024; van Doorn & Badger 2020a, 2020b). As mentioned earlier, employers can use employeesÆ private data as an economic asset and as a basis for training systems that are intended to replace employees.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Employers systematically exploit worker data as an economic asset to consolidate power and automate labor, creating structural imbalances.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that identifies the extraction of surplus value from worker data as a mechanism for reinforcing employer power and labor displacement. Encompasses: Data-driven exploitation, power asymmetry, and automated replacement of labor.

key_points.point: The author proposes that workers should have the right to perform collective data inquiries to audit algorithmic management systems. Because individual explanations are often impossible or meaningless for complex machine learning, collective analysis of aggregate data is necessary to identify discrimination and verify contract compliance. This shifts the power to define and audit system harms to the workers themselves.
key_points.verbatim: Access to such an aggregate view ù which includes enabling interactions of employees with the aggregated datasets ù can assist in auditing whether the parameters provided by the business/software are indeed central parameters in the system.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Grant workers the right to perform collective, aggregate data inquiries to audit and challenge algorithmic management systems.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within skeptic discourse that advocates for empowering workers with collective data access to audit algorithmic systems and ensure accountability. Encompasses: Collective data inquiries, aggregate analysis, and worker-led auditing.

key_points.point: The document highlights that current explanation methods for machine learning are statistically insufficient and cannot guarantee accuracy. Consequently, individual workers cannot rely on these explanations to prove discrimination or appeal unfair decisions. The author argues that only population-level, aggregate data analysis can reveal the true impact of these systems on individuals.
key_points.verbatim: As machine learning systems are based on population-level analysis to determine individual predictions, only population-level data can elucidate a particular decision.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Individual-level AI explanations are technically inadequate for proving harm, necessitating population-level aggregate data analysis.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that asserts the technical failure of individual-level AI explanations to provide actionable recourse for harmed individuals. Encompasses: Statistical insufficiency, population-level analysis, and the inability to prove causation.

key_points.point: The author demands the structural elimination of power disparities in data-driven industries by granting workers collective rights to their data. The document argues that current legal frameworks, such as the GDPR, are insufficient because they focus on individual rights that are difficult to exercise in practice. The author proposes that collective data processing is necessary to counter the exclusive control and value extraction currently held by employers and tech platforms.
key_points.verbatim: The current data industry displays enormous power disparities, human commodification, and exploitation. Both public and private law have difficulty providing suitable theoretical frameworks and starting points for addressing these inequalities and injustices.
key_points.canonical_proposition: It is necessary to establish collective data rights for workers to mitigate power disparities and prevent the exploitation inherent in current data-driven employment models.
key_points.attribution_text: A Desire within skeptic discourse that seeks to rectify systemic power imbalances in the workplace by establishing collective data rights for employees. Encompasses: mitigating human commodification, challenging employer-exclusive data control, and leveraging labor law to address algorithmic exploitation.

key_points.point: The document asserts that algorithmic management systems function as tools of control that exacerbate power imbalances between employers and workers. It argues that current legislation fails to address the reality that machine learning systems are not based on predefined principles, making it impossible for individual workers to understand or challenge the logic of these systems without collective monitoring of data flows.
key_points.verbatim: Machine learning systems are not based on predefined principles. To understand such systems' logic, a continuous and comprehensive look at the outgoing and incoming data flows is needed.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Algorithmic management systems create information asymmetries that systematically shift power from workers to employers, necessitating collective monitoring to achieve transparency.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that algorithmic management systems inherently create power imbalances by obscuring decision-making logic from workers. Encompasses: information asymmetry, the inadequacy of individual transparency rights, and the necessity of collective data monitoring.

key_points.point: The document highlights research on 'collective bargaining on digital platforms' and 'data stewardship' by Kapoor (2021), aligning with the skeptic intention to build shared-ownership structures. By focusing on how workers can organize around data, the document supports the redistribution of power from platform owners to those who produce the data. This approach seeks to institutionalize collective rights as a counterweight to platform-driven exploitation.
key_points.verbatim: Kapoor A. (2021). Collective bargaining on digital platforms and data stewardship. Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Workers and data creators ought to utilize collective bargaining and data stewardship to redistribute power and ownership within digital platforms.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within skeptic discourse that advocates for the implementation of collective bargaining and data stewardship models to redistribute power from platform owners to data producers. Encompasses: Collective bargaining, data stewardship, and platform labor rights.

key_points.point: The document references McQuillan (2018) on 'data science as machinic neoplatonism,' which supports the skeptic belief that AI is often deployed as a technical fix for social problems. This perspective critiques the tendency to treat complex social and political issues as optimization problems solvable by algorithms. It warns against the reductionist nature of applying technical systems to ill-defined social contexts.
key_points.verbatim: McQuillan, D. (2018). Data science as machinic neoplatonism. Philosophy & Technology, 31(2), 253û272.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Data science and AI are frequently deployed as technical fixes for problems that are fundamentally social and political in nature.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that critiques the application of technical optimization frameworks to complex social and political issues. Encompasses: Machinic neoplatonism, technical reductionism, and social-political problem framing.

key_points.point: The document cites research on the 'pathologies of digital consent' by Richards and Hartzog (2019), supporting the skeptic desire for algorithmic transparency as a democratic right. This work argues that current consent models are ineffective and that legal frameworks must move toward mandatory transparency to protect individuals. It emphasizes that consent is often a fiction used to bypass meaningful accountability.
key_points.verbatim: Richards, N., & Hartzog, W. (2019). The pathologies of digital consent. Washington University Law Review, 96(6), 1461û1503.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Legal frameworks ought to replace ineffective digital consent models with mandatory algorithmic transparency to ensure democratic accountability.
key_points.attribution_text: A Desire within skeptic discourse that advocates for the replacement of current digital consent models with mandatory algorithmic transparency to ensure public accountability. Encompasses: Pathologies of consent, algorithmic transparency, and democratic rights.

key_points.point: The document argues that freedom of association in the digital era must include the right to bring data together collectively to pursue common interests. It frames this as a 'data-driven right to assembly,' which is essential for workers to exercise their rights in data-driven environments.

factual_claims.claim: Machine learning systems in the workplace rely on collective and relational data processing, meaning individual data points have little value without being processed alongside aggregate datasets.
The use of workplace personal data by employers as an independent source of profit constitutes social and economic exploitation of workers.

Machine learning systems in the workplace operate on data-based correlations rather than causality or predefined parameters, making traditional transparency reporting of 'main parameters' insufficient for understanding system behavior.
factual_claims.claim_label: Correlation vs Causality in Workplace AI

factual_claims.claim: Current labor laws in the United States show low unionization rates, with only about 10% of employees represented by labor organizations and 6.3% of private sector employees unionized.
The scaling of machine learning datasets is constrained by the finite availability of high-quality human-generated training data.

evidence_criteria.category_criteria: The claim is an empirical prediction based on current research into machine learning scaling laws.
